gancho: Antes de o Linear B ser decifrado, a professora Alice Kober passou anos contando sinais à mão e encheu 180 mil fichas de papel de rascunho. Morreu em 1950, dois anos antes da solução que ajudou a abrir.
explicacao: Alice Kober, americana nascida em 1906, deu aulas no Brooklyn College de 1930 até morrer, com carga horária cheia e uma sala dividida com outras quatro pessoas. Enquanto outros estudiosos começavam tentando adivinhar a língua por trás do Linear B, a escrita das tabuinhas de Creta, ela insistiu em partir do que as próprias tabuinhas mostravam: quantas vezes cada sinal aparecia, em que posição e ao lado de quais outros. Encheu 40 cadernos e, quando a Segunda Guerra deixou o papel escasso, 180 mil fichas feitas de sobras. Em artigos de 1945 e 1946, provou que a língua tinha flexão, com finais de palavra que mudavam, e achou as "sílabas-ponte": com elas, dava para saber quais sinais tinham a mesma consoante ou a mesma vogal sem conhecer o som de nenhum. Em 1948, publicou uma grade com dez sinais organizados assim. Morreu em 1950, aos 43 anos. Michael Ventris partiu dessa base para montar as próprias grades e, em 1952, descobriu que a língua era uma forma arcaica de grego. John Chadwick, parceiro de Ventris, reconheceu que ela lançou os alicerces e chamou o trabalho dela de "o mais valioso" antes da solução final.

fontes.trecho: Alice Elizabeth Kober (December 23, 1906 – May 16, 1950) was an American classicist best known for her work on the decipherment of Linear B. [...] Kober taught classics at Brooklyn College from 1930 until her death. [...] she taught a full course load, sharing an office with four others. [...] Unlike other scholars at the time, who began their analysis of the script by attempting to identify the language that it encoded, Kober believed that any decipherment of Linear B must begin with the internal evidence of the Linear B tablets. She began her work on Linear B by analysing the individual characters on the tablets, compiling statistics about their frequency, the positions they appeared in, and the characters which they appeared alongside. Over the course of her work on the script, she filled 40 notebooks and – after the beginning of the Second World War made paper harder to come by – 180,000 index cards made from scrap paper with her research notes. In 1945, Kober published the first of three major papers on Linear B, "Evidence of Inflection in the 'Chariot' Tablets from Knossos", proving the hypothesis, first suggested by Sir Arthur Evans, that it recorded an inflected language. In 1946 she published the second of her major papers on the script [...] In it, Kober identified so-called bridging syllables, where the beginning of the syllable is part of the root of a word, and the end is part of the inflected suffix; this allowed for the identification of phonetic relationships between sets of Linear B signs. [...] in this article Kober set forth a grid of ten Linear B characters, showing for each which other signs it shared a consonant or vowel with. [...] she submitted the finished manuscript in October 1947, and it was published in 1948. [...] She died on May 16, 1950, aged 43. [...] after Michael Ventris' decipherment of the script, his collaborator John Chadwick recognised her for laying the foundation, and described her contributions to the study of Linear B as "the most valuable" before Ventris' final solution.

Ventris continued with his efforts on Linear B, discovering in 1952 that it was an archaic form of Greek. [...] Alice Kober noted that certain words in Linear B inscriptions had changing word endings – perhaps declensions in the manner of Greek or Latin. Using this basis, Ventris constructed a series of grids associating the symbols on the tablets with consonants and vowels.

gancho: O Linear B foi decifrado por um arquiteto que decidiu enfrentá-lo aos 14 anos, numa palestra. Ele apostava num parentesco com o etrusco. Era grego, "quinhentos anos mais velho que Homero", nas palavras dele.
explicacao: Em 1936, Arthur Evans, que tinha achado as tabuinhas em Cnossos, em Creta, mostrou algumas a um grupo de estudantes numa exposição em Londres. Michael Ventris, de 14 anos, confirmou com ele que a escrita seguia sem decifração e decidiu decifrá-la. Aos 18, publicou um artigo defendendo um parentesco com o etrusco, ideia errada que ele perseguiu até o começo dos anos 1950. Formado em arquitetura, desenhava escolas para o governo. Partindo das tabelas de sinais de Alice Kober, a virada veio de um palpite: certos grupos de sinais apareciam só nas tabuinhas de Creta, e não nas do continente grego. Seriam nomes de lugares da ilha, e eram. Com os sons tirados deles, Ventris percebeu que a língua era grego e anunciou isso pela rádio BBC em 1º de julho de 1952. Entre os ouvintes estava John Chadwick, filólogo de Cambridge, que passou a trabalhar com ele. Uma tabuinha de Pilos achada em 1953 ajudou a convencer: ao lado do desenho de um caldeirão de três pés, os sinais diziam "ti-ri-po-de", tripé. Os textos não são poemas: são registros de palácios, com lã, ovelhas e grãos. Ao contrário do que muita gente supõe, não há indício de que Ventris tenha trabalhado com quebra de códigos na guerra. Ele morreu num acidente de carro em 1956.

fontes.trecho: Michael George Francis Ventris (; 12 July 1922 – 6 September 1956) was an English architect, classicist and philologist who deciphered Linear B, the ancient Mycenaean Greek script. [...] Ventris died in a car crash a few weeks before the publication of Documents in Mycenaean Greek [...] There is also no evidence that he was ever part of any code-breaking unit, as was Chadwick, even though the public has readily believed this explanation of his genius and success with Linear B. [...] He designed schools for the Ministry of Education. [...] In 1936, Evans hosted an exhibition on Cretan archaeology at Burlington House in London [...] Boys from Stowe School were in attendance at one lecture and tour conducted by the 85-year-old Evans himself. Ventris, aged 14 at the time, was present [...] Evans held up tablets of the unknown scripts for the audience to see. During the interview period following the lecture, Ventris spoke up to confirm that Linear B was as yet undeciphered, and he determined to decipher it. In 1940, the 18-year-old Ventris had an article "Introducing the Minoan Language" published in the American Journal of Archaeology. Ventris's initial hypothesis was that Etruscan and Linear B were related and that this might provide a key to decipherment. Although this proved incorrect, it was a link he continued to explore until the early 1950s. [...] Comparing the Linear B tablets discovered on the Greek mainland and noting that certain symbol groups appeared only in the Cretan texts, Ventris made the inspired guess that those were place names on the island. This proved to be correct. Armed with the symbols he could decipher from this, Ventris soon unlocked much of the text and determined that the underlying language of Linear B, a syllabic script, was in fact Greek. On 1 July 1952, Ventris announced his preliminary findings on a BBC radio talk [...] In 1953 further Linear B tablets were discovered at ancient Mycenae and ancient Pylos on the Greek mainland, with one of the tablets (PY Ta 641) showing a pictographic tripod cauldron next to Linear B symbols which were translated by Ventris and Chadwick as "ti-ri-po-de", tripod being a Greek word. [...] which was heard by John Chadwick, a classicist at the University of Cambridge [...] The two men began to collaborate on further research into deciphering Linear B.

with Ventris describing the language of Linear B as "[a] difficult and archaic Greek, seeing that it's five hundred years older than Homer, and written in a rather abbreviated form, but Greek nevertheless." [...] The major cities and palaces used Linear B for records of disbursements of goods. Wool, sheep, and grain were some common items, often given to groups of religious people. [...] His initial decipherment was achieved using Kober's classification tables, to which he applied his own theories.

gancho: Por volta de 1800, um professor alemão apostou com amigos de copo que decifraria inscrições persas em cuneiforme. Leu nomes de reis graças a uma pista: o pai de um deles aparecia sem o título de rei.
explicacao: Georg Friedrich Grotefend dava aulas num colégio de Göttingen e gostava de quebra-cabeças. Escolheu duas inscrições reais de Persépolis, copiadas antes pelo viajante Carsten Niebuhr, que diziam quase a mesma coisa, exceto pelos nomes dos governantes. Friedrich Münter já tinha percebido que um grupo de sinais repetido devia ser a palavra "rei" e que um sinal inclinado separava as palavras. Grotefend juntou a isso o modelo de inscrições de reis persas bem posteriores, em que o nome do soberano vem seguido de "grande rei, rei dos reis" e do nome do pai. Notou que o primeiro nome de uma inscrição reaparecia como pai na outra, e que o pai do outro rei não levava o título real. Pela genealogia conhecida dos gregos, só um caso servia: Dario, o Grande, cujo pai, Histaspes, não foi rei, e cujo filho foi Xerxes. Ao soletrar esses nomes, ele obteve o som de vários sinais. Em 1802, tinha decifrado dez dos 37 sinais do persa antigo. A Sociedade Real de Göttingen, porém, rejeitou o trabalho e não o publicou; ele só saiu em 1815, como apêndice do livro de um amigo.

fontes.trecho: Heyne's recommendation procured for him an assistant mastership in the Göttingen gymnasium in 1797. [...] exact copies of them had been published by Jean Chardin in 1711, the Dutch artist Cornelis de Bruijn and the German traveller Carsten Niebuhr, who lost his eyesight over the work [...] Having a taste for puzzles, he made a bet with drinking friends around 1800 that he could decipher at least part of the Persepolis inscriptions. His first discovery was communicated to the Royal Society of Göttingen in 1802, but his findings were dismissed by these academics. His work was denied official publication [...] In 1815, Grotefend was only able to give an account of his theories in the work of his friend Heeren on ancient history. His article appeared as an appendix in Heeren's book [...] Grotefend had focused on two Achaemenid royal inscriptions from Persepolis, called the "Niebuhr inscriptions", which seemed to have broadly similar content except for the name of the rulers. In 1802, Friedrich Münter had realized that recurring groups of characters must be the word for "king" [...] He also understood from Münter that each word was separated from the next by a slash sign [...] Grotefend extended this work by realizing, based on the known inscriptions of much later rulers (the Pahlavi inscriptions of the Sassanid kings), that a king's name is often followed by "great king, king of kings" and the name of the king's father. [...] he made the hypothesis that the father of the ruler in one inscription would possibly appear as the first name in the other inscription [...] Looking at the length of the character sequences, and comparing with the names and genealogy of the Achaemenid kings as known from the Greeks, also taking into account the fact that the father of one of the rulers in the inscriptions didn't have the attribute "king", he made the correct guess that this could be no other than Darius the Great, his father Hystaspes who was not a king, and his son the famous Xerxes. [...] These connections allowed Grotefend to figure out the cuneiform characters that are part of Darius, Darius's father Hystaspes, and Darius's son Xerxes.
Grotefend had deciphered ten of the 37 symbols of Old Persian by 1802

gancho: Em 1857, para testar se o cuneiforme acadiano estava mesmo decifrado, quatro estudiosos receberam cópias da mesma inscrição recém-achada. As traduções bateram. Um deles era um pioneiro da fotografia.
explicacao: Por volta de 1851, o clérigo irlandês Edward Hincks e o oficial britânico Henry Rawlinson já liam uns 200 sinais acadianos. Parte do caminho veio da inscrição de Behistun, gravada no reinado do persa Dario com o mesmo texto em três línguas do império: persa antigo, babilônio e elamita. Rawlinson concluiu a decifração do persa antigo, iniciada décadas antes por outros, e ele e Hincks, cada um por sua conta, passaram às outras escritas. Mas como provar que as leituras não eram fantasia? Em 1857, Edwin Norris, secretário da Royal Asiatic Society, deu a cada um de quatro estudiosos uma cópia de uma inscrição recém-descoberta do rei assírio Tiglate-Pileser I: Hincks, Rawlinson, o jovem alemão Julius Oppert e William Henry Fox Talbot. Um júri de especialistas examinou as versões e as achou muito próximas nos pontos essenciais. Talbot, menos experiente, errou mais, e as passagens duvidosas de Oppert foram atribuídas, com delicadeza, ao inglês pouco familiar para ele. As de Hincks e Rawlinson coincidiam de forma notável. O júri deu a decifração por concluída. Talbot é o mesmo que inventou o calótipo, processo fotográfico com negativo de papel do qual se tiravam quantas cópias se quisesse. Ele passou 20 anos envolvido com a assiriologia.

fontes.trecho: Meanwhile, in 1835 Henry Rawlinson, a British East India Company army officer, visited the Behistun Inscriptions in Persia. Carved in the reign of King Darius of Persia (522–486 BC), they consisted of identical texts in the three official languages of the empire: Old Persian, Babylonian and Elamite. [...] Rawlinson successfully completed the decipherment of Old Persian cuneiform. [...] After translating Old Persian, Rawlinson and, working independently of him, the Irish Assyriologist Edward Hincks, began to decipher the other cuneiform scripts in the Behistun Inscription. [...] By 1851, Hincks and Rawlinson could read 200 Akkadian signs. They were soon joined by two other decipherers: young German-born scholar Julius Oppert, and versatile British Orientalist William Henry Fox Talbot. In 1857, the four men were requested to take part in a famous experiment to test the accuracy of their decipherments. Edwin Norris, the secretary of the Royal Asiatic Society, gave each of them a copy of a recently discovered inscription from the reign of the Assyrian emperor Tiglath-Pileser I. A jury of experts was impaneled to examine the resulting translations and assess their accuracy, and the results were published. In all essential points, the translations produced by the four scholars were found to be in close agreement with one another. There were, of course, some slight discrepancies. The inexperienced Talbot had made a number of mistakes, and Oppert's translation contained a few doubtful passages which the jury politely ascribed to his unfamiliarity with the English language. But Hincks' and Rawlinson's versions corresponded remarkably closely in many respects. The jury declared itself satisfied, and the decipherment of Akkadian cuneiform was adjudged a fait accompli.
Edward Hincks (19 August 1792 – 3 December 1866) was an Irish Church of Ireland clergyman, Egyptologist and Assyriologist, known for the decipherment of cuneiform.

was an English scientist, inventor, and photography pioneer who invented the salted paper and calotype processes [...] He had a 20-year involvement in the field of Assyriology [...] The translucent calotype negative made it possible to produce as many positive prints as desired by simple contact printing

gancho: A chave do hitita foi uma frase sobre pão e água. O tcheco Bedřich Hrozný notou que "watar" lembrava o inglês "water" e "ezza-" o alemão "essen", comer: a língua era parente distante do português.
explicacao: Em 1906, uma expedição alemã achou em Hattusa, a uns 200 km de Ancara, o arquivo dos reis hititas: tabuinhas num cuneiforme que já se sabia ler, mas numa língua desconhecida. Em 1902, Jørgen Alexander Knudtzon já tinha defendido que o hitita era indo-europeu, com base em duas cartas achadas em Amarna, no Egito, mas sem prova definitiva. Hrozný se concentrou numa passagem: nu NINDA-an ezzatteni watar-ma ekutteni. Sabia-se que NINDA era o sinal sumério para pão. Ele supôs que -an marcasse o objeto direto e que ezza- tivesse a ver com o pão: lembrava o latim edo e o alemão essen, comer. Daí, "vocês comerão pão". Na segunda parte, watar recordava water e Wasser, e eku- parecia o latim aqua: "beberão água". O hitita era, portanto, da mesma família do latim, do grego, do sânscrito e das línguas germânicas. Ele apresentou o argumento num artigo de 1915 e, em 1917, quando estava na ativa no exército austro-húngaro durante a Primeira Guerra, publicou uma gramática. A argumentação era moderna, embora ainda pouco fundamentada, mas foi aceita depressa e reforçada por outros estudiosos.

fontes.trecho: In 1906, at Hattusa (modern Boğazkale, about 200 km east of Ankara) a German expedition found the archives of the Hittite kings in cuneiform, but in an unknown language. While on active duty in the Austro-Hungarian army during World War I, Hrozný published in 1917 a description of the language showing that it belonged to the Indo-European family. [...] To solve the mystery of the Hittite language, Bedřich Hrozný focused on a text passage that reads: nu NINDA-an ezzatteni watar-ma ekutteni. It was known at that time that the ideogram for NINDA meant bread in Sumerian. Hrozný thought that the suffix -an might be the Hittite accusative singular ending. Then, he assumed that the second word, ed-/ezza-, had something to do with the bread and thought that it could be the verb eat. The comparison with Latin edo, English eat, and German essen led him to infer that NINDA-an ezzatteni means "you (will) eat bread". In the second sentence, Hrozný was struck by the word watar, which recalled English water and German Wasser. The last word of the second sentence, ekutteni, had the stem eku-, which seemed to resemble the Latin aqua (water). He thus translated the second sentence as "you (will) drink water". Hrozný soon realized that the Hittites were speaking an Indo-European language

The first substantive claim as to the affiliation of Hittite was made by Jørgen Alexander Knudtzon in 1902, in a book devoted to two letters between the king of Egypt and a Hittite ruler, found at El-Amarna, Egypt. Knudtzon argued that Hittite was Indo-European, largely because of its morphology. [...] He presented his argument that the language is Indo-European in a paper published in 1915 (Hrozný 1915), which was followed by a grammar of the language (Hrozný 1917). Hrozný's argument for the Indo-European affiliation of Hittite was thoroughly modern although poorly substantiated. [...] Hrozný's decipherment, tentative grammatical analysis and demonstration of the Indo-European affiliation of Hittite were rapidly accepted and more broadly substantiated by contemporary scholars

gancho: A chave para ler os maias veio do frade que mandou destruir os livros deles. Um linguista soviético que nunca pisara numa ruína maia percebeu que o "alfabeto" anotado pelo frade era de sílabas.
explicacao: No século XVI, em Iucatã, o frade franciscano espanhol Diego de Landa, que mais tarde seria bispo de Iucatã, comandou a destruição de todos os códices maias que encontrou. Chamado de volta à Espanha para ser julgado, escreveu uma obra para se justificar e nela reproduziu um "alfabeto": as letras espanholas e os glifos maias que, segundo ele, lhes correspondiam. O original sumiu, e uma cópia resumida só foi achada nos anos 1860. Como o alfabeto parecia confuso e contraditório, quem tentou usá-lo como chave fracassou. Em 1952, Yuri Knorozov, então com 30 anos, propôs que se tratava de sílabas: quando Landa pedia a letra "b", o escriba maia desenhava o glifo da sílaba "be", como Landa pronunciava a letra. O "alfabeto" virou quase uma Pedra de Roseta maia. J. Eric S. Thompson, o maianista mais respeitado da época, atacou a ideia, e, segundo Michael Coe, raros ousavam contrariá-lo; a decifração só deslanchou depois da morte dele, em 1975. Coe lembra que Knorozov, antes do fim dos anos 1980, nunca tinha visto uma ruína nem tocado numa inscrição maia real. Em 1990, convidado pelo presidente da Guatemala, visitou Tikal. A história de que ele salvou um livro maia de uma biblioteca em chamas em Berlim é lenda: o próprio Knorozov contou que não houve incêndio e que os livros estavam em caixas.

fontes.trecho: According to a popular legend, Knorozov and his unit supported the push of the Red Army vanguard into Berlin. [...] Supposedly, when stationed in Berlin, Knorozov came across the National Library while it was ablaze. [...] Knorozov himself, in an interview conducted a year before his death, denied the Berlin legend. [...] There wasn't any fire in the library. And the books that were in the library, were in boxes to be sent somewhere else. [...] a record produced by the 16th century Spanish Bishop Diego de Landa in which he claimed to have transliterated the Spanish alphabet into corresponding Maya hieroglyphs. De Landa, who during his posting to Yucatán had overseen the destruction of all the codices from the Maya civilization he could find, reproduced his alphabet in a work (Relación de las Cosas de Yucatán) intended to justify his actions once he had been placed on trial when recalled to Spain. The original document had disappeared, and this work was unknown until 1860s when an abridged copy was discovered [...] Since de Landa's "alphabet" seemed to be contradictory and unclear [...] previous attempts to use this as a key for deciphering the Maya writing system had not been successful. [...] In 1952, the then 30-year-old Knorozov published a paper [...] Knorozov's key insight was to treat the Maya glyphs represented in de Landa's alphabet not as an alphabet, but rather as a syllabary. [...] He maintained that when de Landa commanded his informant to write the equivalent of the Spanish letter "b" (for example), the Maya scribe actually produced the glyph that corresponded to the syllable /be/, as spoken by de Landa. [...] In effect, the de Landa "alphabet" was to become almost the "Rosetta stone" of Mayan decipherment. [...] J. Eric S. Thompson, the noted British scholar regarded by most as the leading Mayanist of his day, led the attack. [...] According to Michael Coe, "during Thompson's lifetime, it was a rare Maya scholar who dared to contradict" him [...] could only take off after Thompson's death in 1975. [...] "Yuri Knorozov, a man who was far removed from the Western scientific establishment and who, prior to the late 1980s, never saw a Mayan ruin nor touch[ed] a real Mayan inscription, had nevertheless, against all odds, made possible the modern decipherment of Maya hieroglyphic writing." [...] After diplomatic relations between Guatemala and the Soviet Union were restored in 1990, Knorozov was invited by President Vinicio Cerezo to visit Guatemala. [...] Knorozov visited several of the major Mayan archaeological sites—including Tikal.

he became a Franciscan friar in 1541, and was sent as one of the first Franciscans to the Yucatán, arriving in 1549. [...] Landa was sent back to Spain by Bishop Toral, to stand trial for conducting an illegal Inquisition. [...] In 1569, the committee absolved Landa of his crimes. Bishop Toral died in Mexico in 1571, allowing King Philip II of Spain to appoint Landa as the second bishop of Yucatán.

gancho: O maior especialista em maias achava que as inscrições deles não registravam história. Uma arquiteta que desenhava ruínas mostrou que as datas das estelas eram nascimentos, posses e mortes de reis.
explicacao: Tatiana Proskouriakoff nasceu em Tomsk, na Rússia, em 1909, e cresceu nos Estados Unidos. Formou-se em arquitetura em 1930, a única mulher da turma, e entrou na arqueologia desenhando as ruínas da cidade maia de Piedras Negras, na Guatemala. Nunca teve diploma em estudos maias. Enquanto estudava como o estilo da escultura maia mudava com o tempo, notou que as datas gravadas nas estelas eram históricas: marcavam o nascimento, a subida ao trono e a morte dos governantes. Pelo padrão das datas e dos glifos, demonstrou uma sequência de sete governantes ao longo de duzentos anos. Os trabalhos, publicados a partir de 1960, contrariavam J. Eric S. Thompson, o maianista mais respeitado da época, para quem as inscrições não registravam a história real, e acabaram por convencê-lo. Conhecendo o contexto, os epigrafistas puderam decifrar os glifos; em 1973, numa mesa-redonda em Palenque, um grupo leu o que se revelou uma lista dos antigos governantes da cidade. Ela morreu em 1985. Em 1998, um colega levou parte das cinzas a Piedras Negras, e elas foram enterradas no alto da acrópole que ela retratara no seu primeiro desenho de reconstrução.

fontes.trecho: 23 January [O.S. 10 January] 1909, – August 30, 1985) was a Russian-American Mayanist scholar [...] Born in Tomsk, Tatiana moved to the US with her parents in 1916. [...] Proskouriakoff's most significant scientific contribution is considered to be the consistent application of the structural method to Mayan inscriptions of the classical period, as a result of which she proved that historical events were recorded on the monuments. Publications about new method application have been published since 1960. [...] In 1926, Tatiana enrolled at the Pennsylvania State College School of Architecture and graduated as the only female in her class in 1930. [...] Tatiana's first assignment at Piedras Negras was to illustrate the architectural ruins of the site. [...] Although Proskouriakoff never received a degree in the field of Maya studies [...] While researching the chronology of changing styles of Maya sculpture, she discovered that the dates shown on the monumental stelae were actually historical, the birth, accession, and death dates for Maya rulers. Analyzing the pattern of dates and hieroglyphs, she was able to demonstrate a sequence of seven rulers who ruled over a span of two hundred years. Knowing the context of the inscriptions, Maya epigraphers were then able to decipher the hieroglyphs. [...] Tatiana Proskouriakoff died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on August 30, 1985. [...] On Easter Sunday 1998, after waiting more than a decade for political tensions to ease along the Usumacinta River, friend and colleague David Stuart carried Tatiana's ashes to Piedras Negras, where they were interred at the summit of the Acropolis, the group of structures in Tania's first and perhaps most famous reconstruction drawing

J. Eric S. Thompson, the noted British scholar regarded by most as the leading Mayanist of his day, led the attack. Thompson's views at that time were solidly anti-phonetic, and his own large body of detailed research had already fleshed-out a view that the Maya inscriptions did not record their actual history [...] The Russian-born but American-resident scholar Tatiana Proskouriakoff was foremost in this work, eventually convincing Thompson and other doubters that historical events were recorded in the script. [...] A major breakthrough came during the first round table or Mesa Redonda conference at the Maya site of Palenque in 1973, when using the syllabic approach those present (mostly) deciphered what turned out to be a list of former rulers of that particular Maya city-state.

gancho: O texto mais longo em etrusco que se conhece sobreviveu nas faixas de uma múmia egípcia. As bandagens ficaram décadas numa vitrine até que, em 1892, um estudioso viu que a escrita era etrusca.
explicacao: Em 1848, Mihajlo Barić, funcionário croata de baixo escalão, comprou no Egito uma múmia de mulher como lembrança de viagem e a deixou em pé num canto da sala, em Viena. Em algum momento tirou as faixas de linho e as expôs numa vitrine separada, aparentemente sem notar a escrita. Depois que ele morreu, o irmão, um padre, doou tudo em 1867 ao atual Museu Arqueológico de Zagreb. No mesmo ano, o egiptólogo Heinrich Brugsch viu o texto, mas o tomou por hieróglifos. Só em 1877 uma conversa com Richard Burton sobre runas o fez perceber que não era egípcio, e os dois concluíram, errado, que era o Livro dos Mortos transcrito em escrita árabe. Em 1892, Jakob Krall identificou a língua como etrusca e remontou as tiras. É o único livro de linho antigo que sobreviveu e, para alguns, o livro mais antigo da Europa: pela escrita, data de cerca de 250 a.C. O pano foi preservado justamente por ter sido usado para enfaixar a múmia no Egito ptolomaico. Como o etrusco ainda é mal compreendido, boa parte do texto segue sem tradução, mas as datas e os nomes de deuses indicam que é um calendário de rituais. Hoje o livro fica numa sala refrigerada do museu.

fontes.trecho: is the longest Etruscan text and the only extant linen book (libri lintei), dated to the 3rd century BC, making it arguably the oldest extant European book. [...] Much of it is untranslated because of the lack of knowledge about the Etruscan language, though the words and phrases which can be understood indicate that the text is most likely a ritual calendar. [...] The fabric of the book was preserved when it was used for mummy wrappings in Ptolemaic Egypt. The mummy was bought in Alexandria in 1848 and since 1867 both the mummy and the manuscript have been kept in Zagreb, Croatia, now in a refrigerated room at the Archaeological Museum. [...] In 1848, Mihajlo Barić (1791–1859), a low ranking Croatian official in the Hungarian Royal Chancellery, resigned his post and embarked upon a tour of several countries, including Egypt. While there, he purchased a female mummy, as a souvenir of his travels. Barić displayed the mummy at his home in Vienna, standing it upright in the corner of his sitting room. At some point he removed the linen wrappings and put them on display in a separate glass case, though it seems he had never noticed the inscriptions or their importance. The mummy remained on display at his home until his death in 1859, when it passed into possession of his brother Ilija, a priest in Slavonia. As he took no interest in the mummy, he donated it in 1867 to the State Institute of Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia in Zagreb (the present-day Archaeological Museum in Zagreb). [...] The mummy and its wrappings were examined the same year by the German Egyptologist Heinrich Brugsch, who noticed the text, but believed them to be Egyptian hieroglyphs. He did not undertake any further research on the text, until 1877, when a chance conversation with Richard Burton about runes made him realise that the writing was not Egyptian. They realised the text was potentially important, but wrongly concluded that it was a transliteration of the Egyptian Book of the Dead in the Arabic script. [...] In 1892, Krall was the first to identify the language as Etruscan and reassemble the strips. [...] On paleographic grounds, the manuscript is dated to approximately 250 BC [...] Both dates and the names of gods are found throughout the text, giving the impression that the book is a religious calendar.

gancho: A escrita do antigo reino de Cuxe, no atual Sudão, foi decifrada em 1909: dá para soletrar os textos. Mas a língua em que foram escritos segue mal compreendida, e nem a família dela é consenso.
explicacao: A partir do século III a.C., o reino de Cuxe, ao sul do Egito, escreveu sua língua com duas escritas: uma cursiva, derivada do demótico egípcio e presente em cerca de 90% das inscrições, e outra monumental, derivada dos hieróglifos. A última inscrição conhecida, num templo em Kalabsha, foi redatada para o século V d.C. Em 1909, o egiptólogo britânico Francis Llewellyn Griffith decifrou a escrita a partir de nomes egípcios grafados em meroítico. Ele percebeu que cada consoante escrita sozinha trazia um "a" embutido, e as outras vogais eram escritas, como nas escritas da Índia surgidas na mesma época. Com isso, os textos podem ser transcritos, mas só se entende uma pequena parte deles, como nomes e algumas palavras: faltam textos bilíngues. Nem a família da língua é ponto pacífico. Há quem a aproxime das línguas afro-asiáticas, como o egípcio; Claude Rilly propõe que pertence ao ramo sudânico oriental, o das línguas núbias. A escrita deixou um eco: o alfabeto do núbio antigo, derivado do grego, adotou três letras do cursivo meroítico. Em 2008, achou-se a primeira dedicatória real completa, que pode ajudar a confirmar ou derrubar hipóteses.

fontes.trecho: The Meroitic script consists of two alphasyllabic scripts developed to write the Meroitic language at the beginning of the Meroitic Period (3rd century BC) of the Kingdom of Kush. The two scripts are Meroitic Cursive, derived from Demotic Egyptian, and Meroitic Hieroglyphs, derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Meroitic Cursive is the most widely attested script, constituting ~90% of all inscriptions [...] The last known Meroitic inscription is the Meroitic Cursive inscription of the Blemmye king, Kharamadoye, from a column in the Temple of Kalabsha (REM 0094), which has recently been re-dated to AD 410/ 450 of the 5th century. [...] The Old Nubian script, derived from the Uncial Greek script, added three Meroitic Cursive letters [...] The script was deciphered in 1909 by Francis Llewellyn Griffith, a British Egyptologist, based on the Meroitic spellings of Egyptian names. However, the Meroitic language itself remains poorly understood. In late 2008, the first complete royal dedication was found, which may help confirm or refute some of the current hypotheses. [...] Meroitic was a type of script called an abugida: The vowel /a/ was not normally written; rather it was assumed whenever a consonant was written alone. [...] All other vowels were overtly written [...] This system is broadly similar to the Indian abugidas that arose around the same time as Meroitic.

It is poorly understood, owing to the scarcity of bilingual texts. [...] Semitist Edward Lipiński (2011) also argues in favour of an Afroasiatic origin for Meroitic, based primarily on vocabulary. Claude Rilly (2004, 2007, 2012, 2016) is the most recent proponent of the Nilo-Saharan idea: he proposes, based on its syntax, morphology, and known vocabulary, that Meroitic is Eastern Sudanic, the Nilo-Saharan family that includes the Nubian languages.

gancho: Uma tabuinha da Ilha de Páscoa com rongorongo, escrita que ninguém sabe ler, é de madeira cortada entre 1493 e 1509, antes dos europeus. Mas a árvore não é da ilha, e a data virou um enigma.
explicacao: O rongorongo sobrevive em menos de 30 objetos de madeira, quase todos tabuinhas recolhidas no fim do século XIX e hoje espalhadas por museus; nenhuma ficou na ilha. Nenhum glifo pode ser lido, e nem está provado que se trate de escrita plena. A tradição oral diz que só uma pequena elite sabia ler, e os primeiros visitantes ouviram que essa elite, de famílias governantes e sacerdotes, foi sequestrada nos ataques de escravagistas peruanos ou morreu nas epidemias seguintes. Nos anos 1870, a população tinha caído para menos de duzentas pessoas, e tabuinhas abandonadas chegaram a virar tábuas de canoa. A dúvida central é se a escrita surgiu antes dos visitantes europeus do século XVIII, ou por influência deles. Num estudo publicado em 2024, pesquisadores dataram por radiocarbono quatro tabuinhas guardadas em Roma. As outras três deram datas bem posteriores, do fim do século XVII em diante, mas a árvore da tabuinha D teria sido derrubada entre 1493 e 1509, data que os próprios autores não esperavam. Há duas ressalvas: datou-se a madeira, não a escrita, que pode ser mais recente; e essa madeira, de uma espécie que não é nativa da ilha, foi reaproveitada, o que, segundo os próprios autores, limita o valor da data. Se o texto for tão antigo e o rongorongo for de fato escrita, seria uma das poucas invenções independentes da escrita, ao lado da Mesopotâmia, do Egito, da China e da Mesoamérica.

fontes.trecho: is a system of glyphs discovered in the 19th century on Easter Island that has the appearance of writing or proto-writing. Numerous attempts at decipherment have been made, but none have been successful. Although some calendrical and what might prove to be genealogical information has been identified, none of the glyphs can actually be read. If rongorongo does prove to be writing and to be an independent invention, it would be one of very few inventions of writing in human history. Two dozen wooden objects bearing rongorongo inscriptions, some heavily weathered, burned, or otherwise damaged, were collected in the late 19th century and are now scattered in museums and private collections. None remain on Easter Island. [...] Oral history suggests that only a small elite was ever literate and that the tablets were sacred. [...] Tablets S and P had been cut into lashed planking for a canoe, which fits the story of a man named Niari who made a canoe out of abandoned tablets. As European-introduced diseases and raids by Peruvian slavers, including a final devastating raid in 1862 and a subsequent smallpox epidemic, had reduced the Rapa Nui population to under two hundred by the 1870s [...] early visitors were told that literacy was a privilege of the ruling families and priests, who were all kidnapped in the Peruvian slaving raids or died soon afterward in the resulting epidemics. [...] The tablets preserved in Rome were carbon-dated in a study published February 2, 2024 [...] It was noted the dating was of the wooden tablet, not of the writing upon it, which could be younger.

fontes.titulo: The invention of writing on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). New radiocarbon dates on the Rongorongo script (Scientific Reports, 2024, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, developed a script, now engraved on fewer than 30 wooden objects, which is still undeciphered. Its origins are also obscure. Central to this issue is whether the script was invented before European travelers reached the island in the eighteenth century AD. [...] Here we radiocarbon-dated four Rongorongo tablets preserved in Rome, Italy. [...] while the others fall within the nineteenth c. AD. [...] Sample number P003 tablet D Échancrée (BRA-6127), including 50 ± 5 years to the felling date, yields an older age compared to the other samples, ranging from 1493 to 1509 cal AD. [...] Such an early age was not expected [...] The chronology of tablet D Échancrée suggests a much earlier horizon, that antedates by centuries the influx of possible external stimuli. [...] the possibility of an independent invention of writing, similarly to what happened in other parts of the world where writing was an original creation, e.g., in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. [...] Given that the tablets A (Tahua) and D (Échancrée) are crafted from wood derived from non-native tree species, it is evident that they were fashioned from repurposed wood, thus limiting their utility in dating the tablet's production and the carvings adorning them [...] Three ranges of the four expand the range of tablets A and B, reaching back to the late seventeenth c. AD.

gancho: Um disco de barro de Creta, da Idade do Bronze, foi "impresso": cada um dos 242 sinais foi feito com um carimbo apertado no barro mole. Ninguém o decifrou, e sem outros textos iguais talvez ninguém consiga.
explicacao: O disco foi achado em 1908 pelo arqueólogo italiano Luigi Pernier, no palácio minoico de Festo, e tem uns 16 cm de diâmetro. Em cada face corre uma espiral de sinais: ao todo, 242 ocorrências de 45 sinais diferentes. O que mais chama a atenção é a técnica: em vez de riscar cada sinal, alguém usou um carimbo para cada símbolo e o pressionou no barro antes da queima. Por isso o disco é visto como um exemplo antigo de impressão com tipos móveis. Jared Diamond o cita como uma inovação que não se espalhou por ter surgido na hora errada, e o compara à prensa de Gutenberg. A data é incerta: as propostas vão de 1850 a 1600 a.C. até depois de 1400 a.C. Por ser tão diferente de tudo, já houve quem suspeitasse de uma fraude de 1908, e a idade nunca foi medida por termoluminescência, mas hoje a maioria dos arqueólogos o aceita como autêntico. Leituras não faltam: grego homérico, hitita, língua semítica, luvita. Nenhuma foi aceita, e nem está claro que seja escrita. Como o texto é curto demais, os especialistas acham improvável decifrá-lo, a menos que os mesmos sinais apareçam em outros lugares.

fontes.trecho: The disc was discovered in 1908 by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier during the excavation of the Minoan palace of Phaistos. The disc is about 16 cm (6.3 in) in diameter and is covered on each side with a spiral text, consisting of a total of 242 occurrences of 45 distinct signs, which were created by pressing individual sign stamps onto the soft clay before firing. While its unique features initially led some scholars to suspect a forgery or hoax, the disc is now generally accepted by archaeologists as authentic. [...] While it is not clear that it is a script, most attempted decipherments assume that it is [...] Yves Duhoux (1977) dates the disc to between 1850 BC and 1600 BC [...] Jeppesen (1963) dates it to after 1400 [...] The most remarkable feature of the Phaistos disc is that the embossed signs that comprise its inscription all result from pressing separate stamps – one for each symbol – into the soft clay before firing. Thus the disc can be seen as an early example of movable-type printing. [...] Popular-science author Jared Diamond describes the disc as an example of a technological innovation that did not become widespread because it was made at the wrong time in history. Diamond contrasts the process with Gutenberg's printing press. [...] scholarly attempts at decipherment are thought to be unlikely to succeed unless more examples of the signs turn up elsewhere, as it is generally thought that there is not enough context available for meaningful analysis. [...] have led some scholars to raise the possibility that the Phaistos disc is a 1908 forgery or hoax. It was pointed out that the date of manufacture has never been established by thermoluminescence dating. [...] Florence Stawell, 1911: interpretation as Homeric Greek, syllabic writing [...] Vladimir I. Georgiev, 1976: interpretation as Hittite language, syllabic writing [...] Kjell Aartun, 1992: interpretation as a Semitic language, syllabic writing [...] Achterberg et al., 2004: interpreted as Luwian.

gancho: Em 2018, um arqueólogo francês usou um truque de dois séculos antes para atacar o elamita linear, escrita da Idade do Bronze: achou nomes de reis em taças de prata. Em 2022, propôs uma decifração quase completa.
explicacao: O elamita linear foi usado em Elão, região vizinha da Mesopotâmia, entre cerca de 2300 e 1850 a.C., ao lado do cuneiforme, para escrever a língua elamita. Em 2021 eram conhecidos só 51 textos e fragmentos. No início do século XX, Ferdinand Bork e Carl Frank compararam uma inscrição bilíngue com o acadiano e fixaram com razoável certeza nove sinais, dos nomes do rei Puzur-Inshushinak e do deus Inshushinak; tentativas seguintes avançaram pouco. Em 2018, François Desset, pesquisador associado do CNRS, estudou taças de prata de uma coleção particular que só vieram a público em 2004. Viu sequências repetidas no início das inscrições e supôs que fossem nomes de reis, mais ou menos como Grotefend fizera com o persa antigo entre 1802 e 1815. Pelo número de sinais e por uma repetição, só dois governantes da época serviam: Shilhaha e Ebarat II, os primeiros reis da dinastia Sukkalmah; outra sequência batia com o deus Napirisha. Isso rendeu novos sinais e, em 2022, uma proposta de decifração quase completa, feita com uma equipe internacional. Para eles, seria o sistema puramente fonético mais antigo conhecido; outros, como o linguista Michael Mäder, veem nele uma parte logográfica. Parte dos especialistas recebeu bem a proposta, e parte aguarda traduções detalhadas.

fontes.trecho: Linear Elamite was a writing system used in Elam during the Bronze Age between c. 2300 and 1850 BCE, and known mainly from a few extant monumental inscriptions. It was used contemporaneously with Elamite cuneiform and records the Elamite language. The French archaeologist François Desset and his colleagues have argued that it is the oldest known purely phonographic writing system, although others, such as the linguist Michael Mäder, have argued that it is partly logographic. [...] Early efforts by Carl Frank (1912) and Ferdinand Bork (1905, 1924) made limited progress. [...] Their proposed near-complete decipherment was published in 2022, being received positively by some researchers while others remain sceptical until detailed translations of texts have been published. [...] As of 2021, there are now 51 known texts and fragments written in Linear Elamite. [...] This permitted a fairly certain determination of nine signs of Linear Elamite: [...] Further efforts were made, but without significant success. [...] Additional readings were proposed by CNRS associate researcher François Desset in 2018, based on his analysis of several silver beakers that were held in a private collection, and only came to light in 2004. Desset identified repetitive sign sequences in the beginning of the inscriptions, and guessed they were names of kings, in a manner somewhat similar to Grotefend's decipherment of Old Persian cuneiform in 1802–1815. Using the small set of letters identified in 1905–1912, the number of symbols in each sequence taken as syllables, and in one instance the repetition of a symbol, Desset was able to identify the only two contemporary historical rulers that matched these conditions: Shilhaha and Ebarat II, the two earliest kings of the Sukkalmah Dynasty. Another set of signs matched the well-known god of the period: Napirisha. [...] In 2020 Desset announced that he and an international team of researchers had completed a proposed decipherment of all known inscriptions in Linear Elamite

gancho: Nos primeiros anos do domínio espanhol no Peru, contadores incas eram chamados aos tribunais, e seus cordões com nós valiam como prova de pagamentos. Hoje, a parte dos quipus que não é número segue indecifrada.
explicacao: Quipu vem de uma palavra quíchua para "nó". Esses conjuntos de cordões floresceram nos Andes entre cerca de 1100 e 1532 e serviram à administração inca para acompanhar impostos, censos, calendário e organização militar. Eram feitos e lidos por especialistas, os quipucamayocs. Depois da conquista, autoridades espanholas recorreram a eles para resolver disputas sobre tributos, e a contabilidade dos quipucamayocs era aceita na justiça. A maior parte da informação dos quipus estudados até hoje é numérica, em sistema decimal. Mas certos nós, as cores, o tipo de fibra e o modo de prender os cordões parecem formar um sistema não numérico ainda indecifrado. Como não se achou ligação clara com nenhuma língua andina, muitos supuseram que os quipus não registram sons. Muitos foram destruídos como idólatras; restam pouco menos de 1.400 pré-colombianos conhecidos. Em 2011, identificou-se uma possível correspondência entre seis quipus coloniais do vale de Santa e um documento espanhol da mesma região, que os pesquisadores consideram a ligação mais próxima de uma Pedra de Roseta já encontrada. E a pesquisadora Sabine Hyland afirma ter feito a primeira decifração fonética, em quipus-cartas de Collata, do século XVIII, mas eles são coloniais e podem ter influência da escrita europeia.

fontes.trecho: Inca administration used quipus extensively for a variety of uses: monitoring tax obligations, collecting census records, keeping calendrical information, military organization [...] flourishing across the Andes from c. 1100 to 1532. [...] However, a recent survey of both museum and private collection inventories places the total number of known extant pre-Columbian quipus at just under 1,400. [...] Many quipus were identified as idolatrous and destroyed [...] The word quipu is derived from a Quechua word meaning 'knot'. [...] Quipus held information, decipherable by officials called quipucamayocs [...] To date, most of the information recorded on the quipus studied by researchers consists of numbers in a decimal system [...] In the early years of the Spanish conquest of Peru, Spanish officials often relied on the quipus to settle disputes over local tribute payments or goods production. The quipucamayocs could be summoned to court, where their bookkeeping was recognised as valid documentation of past payments. Some knots — as well as other features, such as color, fiber type, cord attachments, etc. — are thought to compose an undeciphered non-numeric information system. The lack of a clear link between any indigenous Andean languages and the quipus has historically led to the supposition that quipus are not a glottographic writing system and have no phonetic referent. [...] In 2011, a potential match between six colonial-era Santa Valley Quipus and a Spanish colonial document from the same region was identified. Researchers believe this possible quipu-document match is the strongest Rosetta Stone-like connection currently known [...] Sabine Hyland claims to have made the first phonetic decipherment through her analysis of epistolary quipus from San Juan de Collata, Peru [...] However, the quipus in question date to the colonial period and are believed to have been exchanged during an 18th-century rebellion against the Spanish government, suggesting that their encoding may have been influenced by the introduction of European writing systems.

gancho: Em 1822, Champollion viu uma cópia em que um colecionador inglês sugeria, a lápis, que um cartucho de hieróglifos era o nome de Cleópatra. Adotou a leitura sem explicar como, e o inglês, furioso, cortou a ajuda.
explicacao: O obelisco de Filas, que o colecionador William John Bankes levou do Egito para a Inglaterra, tinha inscrições em grego e em egípcio. Não eram o mesmo texto, como Bankes imaginava, mas ambas citavam Ptolomeu e Cleópatra, e nos hieróglifos esses nomes vinham dentro de cartuchos. O de Ptolomeu já era conhecido pela Pedra de Roseta, onde o britânico Thomas Young, que também atuava em física e medicina, identificara sinais fonéticos. O segundo nome, Bankes só podia adivinhar pelo grego, e anotou o palpite a lápis na cópia. Champollion viu a cópia em janeiro de 1822 e tratou o cartucho como o de Cleópatra, sem nunca explicar como o identificou; havia mais de um caminho possível. Bankes presumiu, furioso, que a sugestão dele fora usada sem crédito e se recusou a ajudá-lo de novo. Comparando os dois nomes, Champollion viu que p, l e o, sinais que propusera para Ptolomeu, cabiam em Cleópatra. O t aparecia com sinais diferentes, e ele concluiu que eram homófonos, sinais distintos com o mesmo som. Depois, testou as letras em outros cartuchos e leu nomes de muitos governantes gregos e romanos do Egito. Ele também foi acusado de usar ideias de Young sem citá-lo. Young, porém, achava que os hieróglifos fonéticos só serviam para palavras estrangeiras.

fontes.trecho: Thomas Young, building on their work, observed that demotic characters were derived from hieroglyphs and identified several of the phonetic signs in demotic. He also identified the meaning of many hieroglyphs, including phonetic glyphs in a cartouche containing the name of an Egyptian king of foreign origin, Ptolemy V. He was convinced, however, that phonetic hieroglyphs were used only in writing non-Egyptian words. [...] His claims were initially met with scepticism and with accusations that he had taken ideas from Young without giving credit [...] Young was a British polymath whose fields of expertise included physics, medicine and linguistics. [...] Young applied these suggestions to the cartouches on the Rosetta Stone. [...] A crucial clue came from the Philae Obelisk, an obelisk bearing both a Greek and an Egyptian inscription. William John Bankes, an English antiquities collector, shipped the obelisk from Egypt to England and copied its inscriptions. These inscriptions were not a single bilingual text like that of the Rosetta Stone, as Bankes assumed, but both inscriptions contained the names "Ptolemy" and "Cleopatra", the hieroglyphic versions being enclosed by cartouches. The Ptolemy cartouche was identifiable based on the Rosetta Stone, but Bankes could only guess based on the Greek text that the second represented Cleopatra's name. His copy of the text suggested this reading of the cartouche in pencil. Champollion, who saw the copy in January 1822, treated the cartouche as that of Cleopatra but never stated how he identified it; he could have done so in more than one way, given the evidence available to him. Bankes angrily assumed Champollion had taken his suggestion without giving credit and refused to give him any further help. Champollion broke down the hieroglyphs in Ptolemy's name differently from Young and found that three of his conjectured phonetic signs—p, l and o—fitted into Cleopatra's cartouche. [...] A fifth sound, t, seemed to be written with different signs in each cartouche, but Champollion decided these signs must be homophones, different signs spelling the same sound. He proceeded to test these letters in other cartouches, identifying the names of many Greek and Roman rulers of Egypt
